title: LASSO — Draw What Your Agent Can Touch
pitch: An AI-assisted dispatch console where a human draws what an agent may understand and change. WebMCP turns that visual scope into a live, typed capability contract.
about_excerpt: An AI-assisted dispatch console where a human draws what an agent may understand and change. WebMCP turns that visual scope into a live, typed capability contract. Like Comment Story Updates LASSO — Draw What Your Agent Can Touch | WebMCP Challenge 2026 Inspiration AI agents are becoming capable of acting inside increasingly complex web applications. But there is still an awkward question: How does a human communicate exactly what the agent is allowed to understand and change? In visual applications such as dispatch maps, dashboards, CAD tools, scheduling boards, and other canvases, the relevant context is often obvious to a human. We can simply point at it. Explaining the same boundary to an agent usually means naming objects manually, writing long instructions, building application-specific permission systems, or trusting the agent to infer intent from the interface. LASSO explores a different interaction model: The human interface generates the agent interface. A dispatcher draws a boundary around the resources the agent may work with. WebMCP turns that transient visual selection into a live, typed capability contract for the visiting agent. The map is the prompt. The boundary is the permission. What it does LASSO is an AI-assisted dispatch console built around a seeded disruption scenario with six late deliveries. The dispatcher draws a freehand lasso around the deliveries and drivers the AI agent may reason about. That gesture does much more than highlight the map. LASSO compiles the selected UI state into revision-specific WebMCP tools whose JSON Schemas contain only the resources inside the human-defined boundary. The external agent then: Inspects the scoped operational state. Authors its own recovery plan. Submits the plan to LASSO for deterministic validation. Receives structured violations if the plan breaks capacity, vehicle, timing, overtime, or scope constraints. May request additional resources outside its current authority. Cannot grant that additional authority to itself. Repairs its plan after the human approves a scope expansion. Can modify live routes only after the human authorizes one exact verified plan. In the demo scenario, the agent discovers that delivery D15 requires refrigerated capacity that is unavailable inside its original scope. It asks for Mika, a suitable driver outside the boundary. The human chooses whether to include Mika. That single UI action invalidates the previous WebMCP contract and compiles a new revision in which Mika becomes available to the agent. The repaired plan reduces six late deliveries to one with three route changes and zero overtime. Only then can the dispatcher authorize execution. The resulting write capability is bound to the exact plan, current scope, workspace generation, and a single expiring use. Stale or replayed authority is rejected. Why WebMCP LASSO is not an optimizer with a tool wrapper. The agent authors the plan . LASSO provides the scoped world model, deterministic validation, authority negotiation, and execution boundary. The central WebMCP idea is that the tool surface itself changes as the human manipulates the live application. A visual gesture becomes structured machine-readable context. When the human changes the lasso, the agent's available resource IDs and capability contract change with it. Traditional browser automation can see a highlighted region, but it still has to infer what that highlight means and whether it represents authority. A conventional remote API or MCP server would require additional synchronization to know what the human just selected in the browser. With WebMCP, the page itself can expose that ephemeral application state directly to the visiting agent. How we built it LASSO is a lightweight, dependency-free web application built with vanilla JavaScript, HTML, CSS, SVG, JSON Schema, and the imperative WebMCP API. The architecture separates four responsibilities: Human UI — visual scope, operational constraints, authority decisions Scope compiler — converts UI state into revision-specific WebMCP contracts External agent — creates and repairs recovery plans Policy engine — validates and safely applies scoped state changes The application also includes deterministic browser, security, adversarial, package, and performance validation. The final local release campaign includes more than 150 correctness and security invariants plus a 5,000-case adversarial fuzz campaign. Challenges The hardest problem was not drawing a lasso. It was making the boundary meaningful. We had to ensure that: changing scope invalidates stale capabilities; an agent cannot expand its own authority; outside-scope assignments remain untouched; a delivery can never silently acquire multiple owners; application handlers validate authority independently of JSON Schema; partially registered WebMCP contracts fail closed; in-flight tool calls are not broken by contract recompilation; an authorized plan cannot be changed and replayed later. Several of these issues only appeared during adversarial testing and required changes to the underlying state-transition model rather than cosmetic fixes. What we learned WebMCP becomes especially interesting when tools are not static API endpoints. A web application's live human state can itself determine what capabilities an agent discovers. That creates a new interaction loop: human gesture → typed capability → agent reasoning → authority request → human decision → new capability The conversation between human and agent does not have to happen entirely in a chat box. The web interface itself can participate. What's next Dispatch is the demonstration, not the limit. The same interaction pattern could apply anywhere humans naturally identify context spatially: operations dashboards analytics CAD and design tools scheduling systems infrastructure maps logistics spreadsheets and visual workspaces The long-term idea is simple: Point at the context. Let the web turn that gesture into an agent contract. video_transcript_excerpt:
Meet Lasso, an AI assisted dispatch console. 
Six deliveries are late. A dispatcher draws   the deliveries and drivers an AI agent may work 
with. WebMCP lets the page turn that gesture into   the agents temporary typed tool set. Inside 
the boundary are six deliveries, two drivers,   no overtime, and at most three route changes. 
The agent receives detailed data only for that   selected operational scope. This is not a visual 
highlight. The generated JS schema contains only   the selected resource ids. Change the map and 
the agents tools change with it. Without webmc,   a browser agent may see the screen, but it cannot 
discover the exact app authored contract the   human just created. The agent authors a recovery 
plan. Lasso does not secretly optimize for it.   It evaluates the proposal and rejects unsafe 
choices. Excess capacity, forbidden overtime,   and no refrigerated vehicle for delivery. D15. 
The agent learns that a suitable resource exists   outside scope and asks for access. It cannot 
expand its own authority. The dispatcher includes   MA. Revision 2 disappears. Revision 3 is compiled, 
now allowing Mika as a driver. The agent repairs   the plan. Before anything changes, lasso proves 
the result. Six late deliveries become one with   three route changes and zero overtime. Only the 
human unlocks execution. The right tool is bound   to this exact plan, this scope, and one expiring 
use. The agent applies it. New routes go live. A   stale call is rejected and every protected route 
outside the lasso remains untouched. Dispatch is   the demonstration. The same pattern works for any 
map, dashboard or canvas where a human must point   to what an agent may understand and change. The 
map is the prompt. The boundary is the permission.

live_observation.first_impression: A dispatch-recovery scenario asks the user to recover a disruption while preserving human control; it shows no active scope, a no-overtime constraint, and a maximum changed-routes selector.
live_observation.action_attempted: Tried the Reset scenario control as a basic interaction before defining a scope.
live_observation.after_state: The page did not expose a usable post-action state through the browser session; no active scope or agent result was observed.
live_observation.notes: The visible controls support the claimed dispatch and constraint workflow, but drawing a scope and agent execution were not verified.
